title: How to Be Rich
author: J. Paul Getty
summary:
Written in 1965 by the man Fortune magazine once called the richest private citizen in the world, *How to Be Rich* is less a technical investing manual than a personal philosophy of wealth from an oilman who built one of the twentieth century's great fortunes. Getty is explicit from the outset that the book's title is deliberately "How to Be Rich," not "How to Get Rich" — his interest is less in step-by-step tactics for accumulating money than in the mindset, character, and way of living that he believes separates people who are merely wealthy from people who are truly rich in the fuller sense of the word.

The book opens with Getty's own account of building the Getty Oil empire, from early wildcatting successes through the drawn-out, legally contentious campaign to gain control of Tidewater Oil, one of the defining battles of his career. He uses this narrative to draw out lessons about perseverance, calculated risk-taking, and the importance of firsthand operational knowledge — Getty is emphatic throughout that he never asked employees to do work he wasn't willing to understand or do himself, and that this hands-on credibility was central to his ability to lead and negotiate effectively.

From there, the book moves into an extended meditation on business leadership and management, covering what Getty believes makes an effective executive, the destructive power of bad habits inside an organization, common blunders that sink otherwise promising businesses, and his views on managing labor relations fairly but firmly. A recurring theme is that competition and even open dissent within an organization sharpen decision-making, and Getty devotes real space to lamenting what he sees as a growing American cultural discomfort with nonconformity and constructive criticism — arguing that a business, and a society, that punishes dissent stagnates.

The book's later sections turn to Getty's views on investing directly — chapters on Wall Street, real estate, and fine art as asset classes, reflecting his own experience as a major collector — before closing with a set of chapters on the philosophy of money itself: the moral responsibilities that come with wealth, the importance of guarding one's individuality against social and corporate pressure to conform, and what Getty calls a genuine "sense of values" that determines whether money makes a person's life better or simply louder. Throughout, Getty writes as a man convinced that character, discipline, and a willingness to be unpopular are the true prerequisites of lasting wealth, and that the specific mechanics of oil drilling or stock picking matter far less than the psychological and moral qualities a person brings to any pursuit of wealth. The result is part memoir, part management philosophy, and part moral argument for a particular vision of individualist, free-enterprise capitalism, written at a moment — the early-to-mid 1960s — when Getty saw those values as under threat from growing conformity and government intervention in American life.

sections.title: How I Made My First Billion
sections.summary:
This opening section functions as Getty's business memoir in miniature, tracing his path from an early wildcatting success in Oklahoma through decades of expansion into one of the world's largest privately controlled oil empires. Its purpose is to ground the book's later philosophical arguments in Getty's own lived experience, establishing his authority to speak on wealth-building.

The chapter recounts pivotal moments including his early oil strikes, his consolidation of family business interests into the Getty Oil Company, and above all the long, hard-fought campaign for control of Tidewater Oil — a process involving proxy fights, lawsuits, and years of patient stock accumulation before Getty interests finally gained a controlling voice. He frames these episodes as illustrations of persistence, the willingness to be patient over years rather than months, and the discipline to keep buying and building a position even when outside observers doubted the strategy would work.

The section closes by pivoting from narrative to argument, positioning Getty's Middle East expansion and global operations by the 1950s as evidence for the free-enterprise, internationally minded business philosophy he'll elaborate on in later chapters — setting up the more instructional chapters that follow on making money and thinking like a millionaire.
keyLessons: Major business wins often come from sustained, multi-year persistence rather than single dramatic moves.
Direct, hands-on operational involvement builds the credibility needed to lead and negotiate effectively.
Being willing to hold an unpopular or slow-building strategy, even under outside skepticism, can be decisive.

sections.title: You Can Make a Million Today
sections.summary:
This chapter broadens the lens from Getty's personal story to a more general argument about the accessibility of wealth-building for the ambitious reader, and its purpose is to counter the assumption that Getty's success was purely a product of luck or inherited advantage.

Getty argues that opportunity in business is less scarce than most people assume, and that what separates people who accumulate wealth from those who don't is largely a matter of recognizing opportunity, being willing to take calculated risks, and possessing the discipline to follow through once a promising opportunity presents itself. He draws on examples from his own era's business landscape to argue that fortunes were still being built in real time by people willing to work hard and think independently, pushing back against a sense of economic pessimism he detected in some of his readers.

The chapter concludes by transitioning into a discussion of the psychological traits — what he calls the "millionaire mentality" — required to actually execute on this opportunity, handing off directly to the next chapter's focus on mindset.
keyLessons: Getty rejects the idea that major wealth-building opportunities were exhausted by an earlier generation.
Recognizing opportunity and having the discipline to follow through matter more than raw luck.
Calculated risk-taking, not recklessness, is what Getty associates with building wealth from a modest starting position.

sections.title: The Millionaire Mentality
sections.summary:
This chapter turns explicitly to psychology, outlining the attitudes and habits of mind Getty believes distinguish people capable of building and sustaining real wealth. Its purpose is to make the case that mindset, not technique, is the true bottleneck for most aspiring wealth-builders.

Getty describes traits including decisiveness, comfort with calculated risk, the ability to detach ego from decision-making, and a refusal to be paralyzed by the fear of failure. He is critical of what he sees as excessive caution and conformity in American business culture, arguing that genuine wealth creation requires a willingness to act independently of consensus opinion, even when that means enduring criticism or short-term setbacks.

The chapter closes Part One by asserting that this mindset is teachable and adoptable by the reader, setting up Part Two's shift toward the practical mechanics of business leadership and management that Getty believes flow from this underlying mentality.
keyLessons: Decisiveness and comfort with calculated risk are, in Getty's view, more valuable than raw intelligence or capital.
Detaching ego from business decisions helps avoid costly, pride-driven mistakes.
Willingness to act against consensus opinion is often necessary for outsized results.

sections.title: What Makes an Executive?
sections.summary:
Opening Part Two, this chapter lays out Getty's theory of effective business leadership, focusing on the practical qualities that separate genuinely capable executives from merely titled ones. Its purpose is to translate the millionaire mentality from Part One into organizational leadership specifically.

Getty argues that the best executives combine deep, firsthand knowledge of the actual work being done in their organization with the ability to delegate and think strategically at a higher level — a combination he considers rare. He is critical of executives who manage entirely from reports and meetings without ever understanding the operational realities their decisions affect, drawing again on his own habit of working alongside employees in the oil fields early in his career.

The chapter closes by linking executive competence directly to habits, previewing the next chapter's argument that the daily, almost invisible habits of a leader and an organization compound into major long-term outcomes.
keyLessons: Effective executives combine hands-on operational knowledge with the ability to delegate and think strategically.
Managing purely from reports and meetings, without operational grounding, is a common executive failure.
Firsthand experience of the actual work builds the credibility needed to lead a team through hard decisions.

sections.title: The Force of Habit
sections.summary:
This chapter examines how individual and organizational habits — both good and destructive — compound over time to shape a business's trajectory. Its purpose is to make the case that discipline in small, repeated behaviors matters as much as any single strategic decision.

Getty discusses how habits of promptness, thoroughness, and financial discipline, cultivated consistently, become powerful competitive advantages, while habits of procrastination, carelessness, or self-indulgence can quietly erode even a well-capitalized business from within. He draws on examples from his own career of small disciplines — attention to detail in contracts, consistency in following through on commitments — that he credits with outsized long-term impact.

The chapter transitions into the following chapter's more specific catalogue of business mistakes, framing bad habits as the root cause of many of the "blunders and booby traps" discussed next.
keyLessons: Small, repeated habits compound into major competitive advantages or liabilities over time.
Financial and operational discipline in day-to-day details often matters more than any single big decision.
Bad organizational habits erode a business quietly, long before the damage becomes visible in the numbers.

sections.title: Business Blunders and Booby Traps
sections.summary:
This chapter catalogues common mistakes Getty observed businesses and executives make, functioning as a kind of cautionary companion to the more aspirational chapters around it. Its purpose is to warn readers away from specific, recurring failure patterns.

He discusses errors such as overexpansion without adequate capital reserves, poor personnel decisions made under time pressure, failure to adapt to changing market conditions, and the danger of surrounding oneself with advisors who simply agree rather than challenge decisions. Getty draws on both his own near-misses and observations of competitors to illustrate how these mistakes typically unfold.

The chapter closes by connecting these organizational failures to the human relationships inside a company, setting up the next chapter's focus on managing personnel and labor relations soundly.
keyLessons: Overexpansion without adequate capital reserves is one of the most common causes of business failure.
Surrounding yourself with advisors who only agree with you removes a critical check on bad decisions.
Failing to adapt to changing market conditions turns past strengths into present liabilities.

sections.title: The Psychology of Sound Personnel Management
sections.summary:
This chapter addresses how to manage people effectively, treating personnel management as a psychological as much as an administrative challenge. Its purpose is to lay out Getty's philosophy on motivating and retaining capable employees.

He argues for treating employees with genuine respect and fairness, providing real incentives tied to performance, and maintaining consistent standards rather than favoritism. Getty draws a direct line between his own willingness to work alongside laborers early in his career and his later ability to manage large workforces credibly, arguing that respect has to be earned through demonstrated understanding of employees' actual working conditions.

The chapter transitions into the following chapter's more specific discussion of labor relations and unions, extending this philosophy of respect into a more institutional and sometimes adversarial context.
keyLessons: Fair, consistent treatment of employees, grounded in real understanding of their work, builds durable loyalty.
Performance-based incentives work better than favoritism at motivating a workforce over time.
Respect from employees has to be earned through demonstrated understanding, not simply claimed by title.

sections.title: Living with Labor
sections.summary:
This chapter extends the personnel discussion into the specific territory of labor relations and unions, an important and sometimes contentious topic in mid-century American industry. Its purpose is to lay out Getty's pragmatic, if firm, philosophy for navigating this relationship.

Getty describes his approach as combining respect for workers' legitimate interests with firmness against demands he considers unreasonable or economically unsustainable, arguing that businesses that cave indiscriminately to every demand or that refuse all negotiation both end up worse off. He draws on specific historical labor disputes from his own career in the oil industry to illustrate this balance.

The chapter closes by broadening from labor specifically to the theme of a business's relationship with external pressures generally, setting up the next chapter's discussion of how a business withstands sustained external attack.
keyLessons: Sustainable labor relations require balancing legitimate worker interests against economic realities, not simply capitulating or refusing to negotiate.
Consistency and firmness in negotiation build a more stable long-term relationship with a workforce than short-term appeasement.
Getty treats labor relations as a strategic discipline requiring the same rigor as any other part of the business.

sections.title: The Businessman at Bay
sections.summary:
This chapter discusses how a business and its leadership withstand sustained external pressure — from competitors, critics, or hostile takeover attempts — drawing heavily on Getty's own experience in the drawn-out Tidewater Oil fight referenced in Chapter 1. Its purpose is to offer a playbook for resilience under prolonged adversarial pressure.

He describes the psychological toll of years-long legal and business battles, and the importance of maintaining conviction in a long-term strategy despite setbacks, negative press, or the doubts of associates. Getty emphasizes patience and the willingness to absorb short-term losses in service of a longer-term position.

The chapter transitions into the final chapter of Part Two, which addresses situations that seem outright impossible to resolve, extending this theme of resilience to its logical extreme.
keyLessons: Long, adversarial business battles require psychological endurance as much as strategic skill.
Maintaining conviction in a long-term position, despite short-term setbacks and criticism, is often decisive.
External pressure and hostile opposition should be treated as a normal, survivable part of ambitious business activity.

sections.title: The Imp of the Impossible
sections.summary:
Closing Part Two, this chapter addresses situations businesspeople face that appear to have no good solution, and Getty's philosophy for approaching apparently impossible problems. Its purpose is to leave readers with a framework for creative problem-solving under extreme constraint.

Getty argues that many "impossible" business problems are actually solvable through unconventional thinking, willingness to consider options others have dismissed, and refusal to accept the first apparent dead end as final. He offers examples from his own career where persistence and creative restructuring turned around situations that appeared hopeless.

The chapter closes Part Two and transitions into Part Three's broader cultural argument about dissent and nonconformity, framing the willingness to keep searching for unconventional solutions as itself a form of the nonconformity Getty is about to defend at length.
keyLessons: Many apparently "impossible" business problems yield to unconventional approaches that haven't yet been tried.
Refusing to accept the first dead end as final is a distinct, learnable discipline.
Creative problem-solving under extreme constraint is where some of the most valuable business wins originate.

sections.title: The Vanishing Americans
sections.summary:
Opening Part Three, this chapter is a cultural critique arguing that mid-century America was losing its tolerance for genuine individualism and dissent. Its purpose is to set up Getty's broader argument that a healthy business culture depends on a healthy tolerance for nonconformity in the wider society.

Getty laments what he sees as growing social pressure toward conformity — in dress, opinion, and lifestyle — and argues that this cultural homogenization was quietly undermining the entrepreneurial, risk-taking spirit that built companies like his own. He frames this as a historical shift, contrasting what he sees as the rugged individualism of earlier American business generations with a more conformist, security-seeking mid-century mindset.

The chapter transitions into the next chapter's more specific critique of American education and intellectual culture, extending the conformity argument into how the next generation is being shaped.
keyLessons: Getty saw social pressure toward conformity as a direct threat to the entrepreneurial spirit that drives wealth creation.
He frames individualism and comfort with being an outlier as a competitive advantage, not just a personal preference.
Cultural shifts toward conformity and security-seeking, in his view, quietly erode a society's capacity for bold business risk-taking.

sections.title: The Educated Barbarians
sections.summary:
This chapter extends Getty's cultural critique specifically to American education, which he argues was producing technically credentialed people who nonetheless lacked genuine intellectual independence and cultural depth. Its purpose is to locate the roots of the conformity problem in the education system.

He criticizes what he sees as an overemphasis on credentialing and specialization at the expense of broad, independent thinking, arguing that this produces graduates well equipped to follow procedures but poorly equipped to challenge assumptions or generate genuinely new ideas — a trait he considers essential to both business and cultural vitality.

The chapter closes by connecting educational conformity to the next chapter's discussion of a broader "homogenized" American character, continuing the throughline from individual mindset through institutions to national culture.
keyLessons: Getty distinguishes credentialed competence from genuine intellectual independence, valuing the latter more highly.
Overemphasis on specialization, in his view, can come at the cost of the broad, independent thinking that drives innovation.
He treats education's role in either fostering or suppressing independent thought as a matter of real economic consequence.

sections.title: The Homogenized Man
sections.summary:
Closing Part Three, this chapter generalizes Getty's cultural critique into a portrait of a broader "homogenized" American character he sees emerging — risk-averse, conformist, and oriented toward security rather than achievement. Its purpose is to bring the cultural argument to its fullest statement before the book pivots to concrete investment advice.

Getty argues that this homogenization shows up not just in business but in consumer culture, media, and social life, and that reversing it requires individuals to consciously resist pressure to conform in matters of both opinion and lifestyle. He positions his own career and outspokenness as a deliberate rejection of this trend.

The chapter transitions into Part Four's shift toward practical investment guidance, implicitly framing the independent-minded investor as another expression of the nonconformist spirit Getty has just spent three chapters defending.
keyLessons: Getty views cultural and consumer conformity as connected to, not separate from, economic risk-aversion.
He treats deliberate resistance to social pressure as a personal discipline worth cultivating.
His own public outspokenness is framed as a practical demonstration of the nonconformist values he's defending.

sections.title: The Wall Street Investor
sections.summary:
Opening Part Four, this chapter turns to Getty's views on stock market investing, informed by his own decades of experience acquiring and trading positions in companies including his long campaign for Tidewater Oil. Its purpose is to offer the reader concrete, if dated, guidance on equities.

Getty discusses the discipline required for long-term stock investing, warning against speculation driven by short-term market sentiment and advocating instead for careful analysis of a company's underlying fundamentals and management quality before taking a position. He draws on his own experience patiently accumulating stock positions over years, tying the chapter back to the persistence theme from Part One.

The chapter transitions into the next chapter's parallel discussion of real estate as an investment class, continuing Part Four's survey of different asset types.
keyLessons: Getty favors long-term, fundamentals-driven investing over short-term speculation.
He treats patient accumulation of a position over years as a legitimate and often superior investment strategy.
Evaluating management quality, not just financial statements, is central to his approach to picking stocks.

sections.title: A Real Approach to Real Estate
sections.summary:
This chapter covers Getty's views on real estate as an investment vehicle, drawing on his personal experience as a major property owner and developer. Its purpose is to extend the book's investment guidance into a second asset class.

He discusses location, long-term appreciation, and the discipline of buying property based on intrinsic value and future potential rather than speculative trends, cautioning against overleveraging in real estate specifically. Getty situates real estate as a complementary holding to equities within a broader, diversified approach to preserving and growing wealth.

The chapter transitions into the following chapter's discussion of fine art, the final and most personal of the three asset classes Getty covers, given his own extensive art collecting.
keyLessons: Getty applies the same fundamentals-over-speculation discipline to real estate that he applies to stocks.
He warns specifically against overleveraging in property investment.
Real estate is positioned as a complementary, diversifying holding alongside equities, not a replacement for them.

sections.title: Fine Art: The Finest Investment
sections.summary:
Closing Part Four, this chapter reflects Getty's personal passion as one of the era's most significant art collectors, making the case for fine art as both a cultural pursuit and a legitimate long-term investment. Its purpose is to close out the book's investment section on Getty's most distinctive area of expertise.

He discusses the criteria he used for evaluating art purchases, blending genuine aesthetic appreciation with an investor's attention to provenance, scarcity, and long-term value appreciation, and argues that art offers a form of wealth preservation distinct from financial markets. Getty's own collection, later forming the core of the Getty Museum, underlies this chapter's authority.

The chapter transitions into Part Five's closing meditation on the philosophy of money and values, moving from the practical mechanics of investing into the moral and personal dimensions of wealth.
keyLessons: Getty treats fine art as a legitimate long-term asset class, not merely a personal indulgence.
Provenance, scarcity, and genuine aesthetic quality inform his approach to art as an investment.
Art collecting, in his view, offers a form of wealth preservation distinct from and complementary to financial markets.

sections.title: The Morals of Money
sections.summary:
Opening Part Five, this chapter turns explicitly to the ethical responsibilities that Getty believes accompany significant wealth. Its purpose is to prevent the book from ending as a pure how-to guide, insisting instead on a moral dimension to being rich.

Getty argues that wealth carries obligations — toward employees, toward society, toward using resources productively rather than ostentatiously — and criticizes both reckless materialism and the opposite extreme of treating wealth as inherently corrupting. He positions responsible stewardship of wealth as a mark of genuine character.

The chapter transitions into the next chapter's focus on individuality, connecting moral responsibility to the personal integrity required to exercise it well.
keyLessons: Getty frames wealth as carrying real obligations, not simply personal entitlements.
He rejects both reckless materialism and blanket condemnation of wealth as equally simplistic positions.
Responsible stewardship of money, in his view, is itself a mark of character.

sections.title: The Art of Individuality
sections.summary:
This chapter returns to and deepens the book's individualism theme, arguing that guarding one's own values and judgment against social and organizational pressure to conform is essential to both business success and a genuinely rich life. Its purpose is to connect the cultural critique from Part Three back to personal practice.

Getty describes the discipline of maintaining independent judgment even within a large organization or amid social pressure, arguing that many people compromise their individuality gradually and almost unconsciously in pursuit of security or approval. He frames his own career choices as evidence of the value of resisting that drift.

The chapter transitions into the book's final chapter, which broadens individuality into a more general "sense of values" as the ultimate measure of a rich life.
keyLessons: Individuality and independent judgment, in Getty's view, are actively eroded by unconscious drift toward social approval.
Maintaining independent judgment inside a large organization requires ongoing, deliberate effort.
He treats guarding one's individuality as inseparable from both business success and personal fulfillment.

sections.title: A Sense of Values
sections.summary:
The book's closing chapter brings together its business, cultural, and moral threads into a final statement on what it actually means to be "rich" in the fullest sense Getty intends. Its purpose is to leave the reader with the book's ultimate thesis.

Getty argues that money alone does not constitute richness — that a genuinely rich life requires a clear, consciously examined set of values that determine how money, time, and opportunity are used. He closes by returning to the book's title distinction between "getting" and "being" rich, arguing that the habits, character, and values developed along the way matter more than the final balance sheet.

The chapter, and the book, ends by reasserting that the preceding chapters on business tactics and investment were always in service of this larger point about character and values, not ends in themselves.
keyLessons: Getty's final argument is that money without a clear, examined set of values does not constitute being genuinely "rich."
The character and habits built while pursuing wealth matter as much as the wealth itself.
The book's practical business and investment guidance is framed throughout as subordinate to this larger values-based thesis.
Build genuine, hands-on operational knowledge of your business rather than managing purely from reports.
Treat small daily habits of discipline as compounding assets, not minor details.
Surround yourself with people willing to disagree with you, not just people who confirm your decisions.
Approach investing (stocks, real estate, or art) with a long-term, fundamentals-driven mindset rather than chasing short-term trends.
Guard your independent judgment deliberately against social and organizational pressure to conform.
Treat significant wealth as carrying real obligations to employees and society, not just personal entitlements.
Persistence over years, not months, is often what separates successful ventures from abandoned ones.
Define your own "sense of values" so that wealth serves a life you've actually examined, rather than becoming an end in itself.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Being Rich vs. Getting Rich
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Getty's foundational distinction between the mechanics of accumulating money ("getting rich") and the character, values, and way of living that make wealth meaningful ("being rich"). The book is explicitly oriented toward the latter, arguing that money without the right values and habits does not constitute genuine richness.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: Preface and A Sense of Values

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Millionaire Mentality
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Getty's term for the cluster of psychological traits — decisiveness, comfort with calculated risk, ego-detachment in decision-making, and willingness to act against consensus — that he believes are the true prerequisite for building significant wealth, more important than any specific technique or industry.

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Homogenized Man
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Getty's critique of what he saw as a growing mid-century American tendency toward conformity in opinion, lifestyle, and business risk-taking, which he argues actively undermines both entrepreneurial vitality and individual fulfillment.

actionSteps: Identify one area of your business or work where you're managing purely from reports, and spend a defined period doing the actual frontline work yourself to rebuild operational credibility.
List three small daily habits (financial, operational, or personal) you could tighten this month, treating them as compounding assets rather than minor details.
Deliberately add one person to your closest circle of advisors who is willing to openly disagree with your decisions, and ask them to do so on your next major choice.
Before your next investment decision (stocks, property, or otherwise), write down the underlying fundamentals driving it, separate from any short-term market sentiment.
Write a one-paragraph personal "sense of values" statement describing what wealth is actually meant to serve in your life, and revisit it the next time a major financial decision comes up.
reflectionQuestions: Where in your life or business have you drifted toward conformity or security-seeking without consciously deciding to?
What obligations, if any, do you believe come with financial success, and are you currently living up to your own standard?
Which of your current habits, if continued unchanged for ten years, would compound into the biggest advantage — or the biggest liability?

points: Getty's investment chapters on Wall Street, real estate, and fine art reflect market conditions and instruments from the early-to-mid 1960s, well before major shifts like index investing, modern portfolio theory's mainstream adoption, and today's real estate and art markets — several reader reviews note this material reads as the most dated part of the book.

The book is written almost entirely from and for a male executive's perspective, with essentially no engagement with women as businesspeople or investors, which several contemporary readers have flagged as a significant limitation of its "millionaire mentality" framing.

Getty's cultural critique in Part Three (conformity, education, "the homogenized man") is presented as broad social commentary with little empirical grounding, reflecting personal observation and mid-century anxieties about conformity rather than rigorous analysis.

As a memoir-adjacent business book, the narrative naturally centers Getty's own decisions in the most favorable light, particularly around the contentious Tidewater Oil fight, and offers little space to competing perspectives on those same events.

Because Getty inherited substantial early advantages (his father was already a successful oilman who staked his first ventures), some of the "opportunity is available to anyone" framing in the early chapters understates the specific advantages of Getty's own starting position.
criticalTake.contextNote: As both a period artifact and personal philosophy, the book has aged into more of a historical business-culture document than a practical investment guide — its enduring value lies in the character and leadership arguments rather than the specific 1960s-era financial mechanics.

whoThisIsFor: Readers interested in mid-century American business history and in wealth as a matter of character and philosophy, rather than readers looking for current, actionable investment tactics.
whenToReadThis: Read it as a historical business memoir and leadership philosophy, ideally alongside more current investment guides for practical, up-to-date financial tactics.

authorBio.name: J. Paul Getty
authorBio.bio:
J. Paul Getty (1892–1976) was an American oil industry magnate who built the Getty Oil Company into one of the largest privately controlled oil enterprises in the world, and who was for a period regarded as the richest private citizen alive. Born in Minneapolis to a family already established in the oil business, he began his own career in the Oklahoma oil fields before expanding operations globally, including major Middle East concessions that proved transformative to his fortune.

Beyond the oil business, Getty became one of the twentieth century's most significant art collectors, amassing a substantial collection of European paintings and antiquities. That collection became the founding core of the J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles, and the associated J. Paul Getty Trust remains one of the largest arts philanthropies in the world.

Getty was also a prolific, if idiosyncratic, business writer, producing several books that blended memoir, management philosophy, and cultural commentary drawn from his decades running a major international enterprise. He died in 1976 at his English estate, Sutton Place.
